itineraryStops.name: Tongdosa Temple (UNESCO Sansa + Jajangmae plum tree)
itineraryStops.description: **Tongdosa Temple (통도사) — UNESCO World Heritage 'Sansa, Buddhist Mountain Monasteries in Korea' (inscribed 2018)** — is one of the **Three Jewel Temples of Korean Buddhism**, representing the **Buddha (Bul) himself** (the other two are Haeinsa = Dharma/teachings, Songgwangsa = Sangha/community). Founded **646 CE by Master Jajang (자장율사)** during the 15th year of Queen Seondeok's reign, immediately after Jajang's return from Tang China bearing **genuine relics of the historical Buddha** — a robe, a begging bowl, and a bone fragment from the Buddha's skull. These relics are enshrined in the **Geumgang Gyedan (Diamond Stairway)** behind Daeungjeon, and are why **Tongdosa's main hall famously contains NO Buddha image** — the genuine sarira IS the Buddha. The complex is **Korea's largest temple** with 65 buildings + 17 hermitages on Yeongchuksan Mountain (named after India's Mount Grdhrakūta where the Buddha gave the Lotus Sutra teachings; the Korean mountain supposedly resembles the Indian one). **Daeungjeon = National Treasure No. 290** — uniquely with NO Buddha image inside, only an altar facing the Diamond Stairway. The temple was nearly destroyed in the **1592 Imjin War**; only Daeungjeon survived; rebuilding began 1603 and continued through ~17th-19th centuries. The route's seasonal anchor: **Jajangmae (지장매) plum tree** — a **350+ year-old red plum** named after Master Jajang, planted by hand and known as **'the first messenger of spring' in Korean Buddhism**, peak bloom **late February to early March** (year-dependent). Photographers come from across Korea for this single tree against the temple's wooden eaves. Other highlights: **Iljumun gate** + **riverside 1.2 km pine-forest approach** (curved 'dragon-branch' red pines); **Seongbo Museum (Korea's first Buddhist museum)** with 30,000+ artifacts including 600+ Buddhist paintings; **Diamond Stairway** behind Daeungjeon enshrining the genuine Buddha relics. **Temple grounds FREE; Seongbo Museum ~₩2,000-3,000**. **Hours outdoor 24h, Daeungjeon daylight; museum 09:00-17:00, closed Mondays**.

itineraryStops.name: Lunch — Wondong Minari Samgyeopsal (plum season) or Gyeongju
itineraryStops.description: Lunch is at one of two coach-friendly options depending on the season and routing: (1) **Wondong-myeon Minari (미나리) Samgyeopsal** — Wondong township is famous across Korea for **dropwort (Korean water-celery / minari) farms**, peaking from **February to April**. The signature dish: thick-cut samgyeopsal pork belly grilled tableside and wrapped in fresh raw minari (~₩15,000-20,000 per person, traditionally served with soju). The minari season conveniently overlaps with Tongdosa's plum-blossom season — a natural seasonal pairing that locals know but few foreign tourists discover. Or (2) **Gyeongju local restaurant** if the day is running behind schedule or if minari is out of season — Gyeongju ssambap (Korean wrap-and-eat set meal) ~₩13,000-18,000 per person, or the heritage **Gyodong Beopju** rice wine + traditional set menu at Yosukgung 1779 in Gyochon Hanok Village (~₩30,000-50,000 set, premium option). Lunch is at the guest's own expense; vegetarian + halal-friendly options are limited at samgyeopsal restaurants — please notify the guide at booking if dietary accommodations are needed and a substitute (typically a bibimbap or hansik buffet) will be arranged.

itineraryStops.name: Bulguksa Temple (UNESCO World Heritage)
itineraryStops.description: **Bulguksa Temple (불국사) — UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995** (jointly with Seokguram Grotto) — is **the masterpiece of Unified Silla Buddhist art** and **Korea's Historic and Scenic Site No. 1**. Originally built in **528 CE under King Beopheung**, the current grand layout was commissioned in **751 CE by Prime Minister Kim Daeseong** (to honor his earthly parents) and completed in **774 CE** after his death. The temple's name translates **'Temple of the Buddha Land'** — its stone-terrace layout maps Buddhist cosmology in three zones: **Daeungjeon (Hall of Great Enlightenment)** for the historical Buddha, **Geuknakjeon (Hall of Pure Land)** for Amitabha, and **Birojeon (Hall of Vairocana)** for the cosmic Buddha. The wooden halls were destroyed by fire in the **1592-1598 Imjin War**; rebuilding spanned 1604-1805, and the **major modern restoration was 1969-1973 under President Park Chung-hee**. Bulguksa houses **six Korean National Treasures**: **Dabotap (NT 20, 10.4 m, on Korea's 10-won coin)**, **Seokgatap (NT 21, 8.2 m, inside which the world's oldest extant woodblock-printed text — the Pure Light Dharani Sutra dated 704-751 CE — was discovered in 1966)**, the **Cheongungyo + Baegungyo bridges (NT 23, the symbolic 34-step path to enlightenment leading to Jahamun gate)**, the **Yeonhwagyo + Chilbogyo bridges (NT 22, leading to Geuknakjeon Pure Land Hall)**, and the **gilt-bronze Vairocana (NT 26)** + **gilt-bronze Maitreya (NT 27)**. **Admission has been FREE since 2023** under the revised Cultural Heritage Protection Act. The visit follows the temple's pilgrimage axis: **Iljumun gate → Cheongungyo/Baegungyo bridges (admire from below; foot traffic banned) → Jahamun Gate → Daeungjeon courtyard with Dabotap and Seokgatap → Birojeon → Geuknakjeon**. **Hours daily 09:00-18:00 (last admission 17:00)**. **Modest dress + remove shoes when entering halls** + **no drone photography**.

itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: The route's **single most significant cultural anchor** — Bulguksa is the essential UNESCO site for any Gyeongju day tour. Pairing Bulguksa with Tongdosa in the same day is unusual but powerful: both sites are **Master Jajang's spiritual lineage** (Tongdosa founded 646 CE by Jajang; Bulguksa expanded by his successors a century later), making this tour effectively a **'Three Jewel Temple → Buddha Land Temple' pilgrimage** spanning ~125 years of Silla Buddhist history. The 12:45 arrival catches Bulguksa during its post-lunch lull (the busiest 10:00-12:00 tour-bus window has passed) with golden afternoon light on the stone pagodas, the temple's most photogenic time.

itineraryStops.name: Bomun Lake (cherry blossom centerpiece)
itineraryStops.description: **Bomun Lake (보문호)** anchors the **Bomun Tourist Complex** — **Korea's first comprehensive large-scale resort, opened April 6, 1979** under the Gyeongju Comprehensive Development Plan. The Watermill Square plaque reads, '**The History of Tourism in Korea Begins Here.**' The man-made lake covers 1,652,900 m², encircled by a flat **~8 km paved walking & cycling loop** lined with **~2,800 cherry trees** that during peak bloom (last week of March / first week of April) form one of Korea's most photographed cherry-blossom tunnels. **CNN named Bomunjeong (the wooden lakeside pavilion) one of '50 Most Beautiful Places in Korea'** and the lake gained K-pop fame as the filming location for **BTS's 'Butterfly' music video**. The Bomun Tourist Complex spans 793 hectares and includes 10+ international hotels (Hilton Gyeongju 1991, Lahan Select Gyeongju), Gyeongju World amusement park, K-POP Museum, the Donggung Botanical Garden (2013), and the **HICO Convention Center which hosted the 2025 APEC Summit**. The visit samples a **1.5-2 km segment** of the loop on foot: start at Bomunjeong Pavilion → lakeside cherry-blossom path → pause at Watermill Square + 12-m artificial waterfall + tourism plaque → reassemble at coach. Optional **paddle boat or tandem-bike rental ~₩10,000/3hr** if guests want water-level photos. Late-afternoon light on the cherry blossoms reflected in the lake is the day's photographic climax. **Outdoor 24h, FREE; festival illumination ~sunset to 22:00 in early April**. The cherry blossom peak typically falls in the **last week of March through the first week of April**.

routeLogicSections.title: Why a dual-season plum + cherry tour wins

items.label: Plum + cherry are 2–3 weeks apart
items.detail: Plum blossoms (매화) peak ~early March; cherry blossoms (벚꽃) peak ~late March / early April. Most blossom tours commit to one season. This tour's wider operating window (~Feb 25 – Apr 10) and Yangsan + Gyeongju geography lets the daily route adjust to whichever season is currently in peak.

items.label: Tongdosa anchors both seasons
items.detail: The 350-year Jajangmae plum tree at Tongdosa peaks in early March; the temple grounds also have cherry trees that bloom in late March. So Tongdosa is the only stop that delivers regardless of which side of the season you book.

items.label: Yangsan + Gyeongju geography is route-efficient
items.detail: Yangsan is on the way from Busan to Gyeongju (Busan → Tongdosa ~25 min → Wondong ~15 min → Gyeongju ~50 min). The dual-city day is geographically tight, no doubling back.

routeLogicSections.title: Why this is genuinely cultural, not just a flower tour

items.label: Two UNESCO temples in one day
items.detail: Tongdosa (UNESCO Sansa, 2018, Three Jewel Temple) + Bulguksa (UNESCO World Heritage, 1995, six National Treasures) — these are two of Korea's most important Buddhist temples, and visiting both in one day delivers the 'Three Jewel + Mountain Monasteries' narrative arc.

items.label: Tongdosa's unique 'no Buddha image' Daeungjeon
items.detail: Daeungjeon (National Treasure #290) is the only major Korean Buddhist hall without a Buddha image inside — instead the altar faces the Diamond Stairway behind, where Master Jajang enshrined actual Buddha relics in 646 AD.

items.label: 350-year-old plum tree with a name
items.detail: Jajangmae (지장매) is named after Master Jajang himself. It has been the 'first messenger of spring' for 350+ years and is a designated cultural element of the temple, not just decoration.

itineraryStops.name: Tongdosa Temple (UNESCO Sansa + Jajangmae plum tree)
itineraryStops.description: Tongdosa Temple (통도사) is a UNESCO World Heritage 'Sansa, Buddhist Mountain Monasteries in Korea' site (inscribed 2018) and one of the Three Jewel Temples of Korean Buddhism — representing the Buddha himself. Founded 646 CE by Master Jajang, who returned from Tang China bearing genuine relics of the historical Buddha; those relics are enshrined in the Geumgang Gyedan (Diamond Stairway) behind Daeungjeon. That is why Tongdosa's main hall famously contains no Buddha image — the altar faces the relics directly. Daeungjeon is National Treasure No. 290. The complex is Korea's largest temple with 65 buildings + 17 hermitages on Yeongchuksan. The seasonal anchor: Jajangmae (지장매), a 350+ year-old red plum named after Master Jajang, called 'the first messenger of spring' in Korean Buddhism, with peak bloom in late February to early March. The 1.2 km riverside pine-forest approach (curved 'dragon-branch' red pines) is part of the visit. Temple grounds free; Seongbo Museum ~₩2,000–3,000.

itineraryStops.name: Bulguksa Temple (UNESCO World Heritage)
itineraryStops.description: Bulguksa Temple (불국사) is UNESCO World Heritage since 1995 (inscribed jointly with Seokguram Grotto) and Korea's Historic and Scenic Site No. 1. Originally built in 528 CE under King Beopheung, the current grand layout was commissioned in 751 CE by Prime Minister Kim Daeseong and completed in 774 CE. The wooden halls were destroyed in the 1592–98 Imjin War; rebuilding spanned 1604–1805, with major modern restoration in 1969–73. Bulguksa houses six Korean National Treasures: Dabotap (NT 20, on Korea's 10-won coin), Seokgatap (NT 21, inside which the world's oldest extant woodblock-printed text, the Pure Light Dharani Sutra, was discovered in 1966), the Cheongungyo + Baegungyo bridges (NT 23), the Yeonhwagyo + Chilbogyo bridges (NT 22), and the gilt-bronze Vairocana (NT 26) and Maitreya (NT 27). Admission has been free since 2023 under the revised Cultural Heritage Protection Act. Hours daily 09:00–18:00 (last admission 17:00); modest dress and remove shoes when entering halls; no drone photography.

itineraryStops.description: Bomun Lake (보문호) anchors the Bomun Tourist Complex — Korea's first comprehensive large-scale resort, opened April 6, 1979. The HICO Convention Center on the lake hosted the 2025 APEC Summit. The visit samples a 1.5–2 km segment of the loop on foot: Bomunjeong Pavilion → lakeside cherry-blossom path → pause at Watermill Square + 12-m artificial waterfall + tourism plaque → reassemble at coach. routeLogicSections.title: Why this dual-season plum + cherry day works

items.label: Plum and cherry are 2–3 weeks apart — and this tour catches both
items.detail: Plum blossoms (매화) typically peak in early March; cherry blossoms (벚꽃) typically peak in late March to early April. Most spring tours commit to one season. This route's wider Feb 25 – Apr 10 window and Yangsan + Gyeongju geography lets the daily emphasis shift to whichever side is currently at peak, with a mid-March overlap zone where both bloom together.

items.label: Two UNESCO temples in one day
items.detail: Tongdosa (UNESCO Sansa, 2018, Three Jewel Temple representing the Buddha) and Bulguksa (UNESCO World Heritage, 1995, six National Treasures) are two of Korea's most important Buddhist temples. Visiting both in one day delivers the 'Three Jewel + Mountain Monasteries' narrative arc, with roughly 125 years of Silla Buddhist history between Master Jajang's 646 CE foundation at Tongdosa and Kim Daeseong's 751 CE expansion of Bulguksa.

items.label: Tongdosa anchors both seasons
items.detail: The 350-year Jajangmae plum tree at Tongdosa peaks in early March; the temple grounds also have cherry trees that bloom in late March. So Tongdosa is the single stop that delivers regardless of which side of the season you book — even in mid-season days when one bloom is winding down and the other is just starting.

items.label: Yangsan + Gyeongju geography is route-efficient
items.detail: Yangsan sits directly on the way from Busan to Gyeongju (Busan → Tongdosa ~25 min → Wondong ~10 min → Gyeongju ~50 min). The dual-city day is geographically tight, no doubling back. That same routing makes the Wondong minari lunch a natural pause rather than a detour.

items.label: Bomun Lake closes the day at golden hour
items.detail: Placing Bomun as the final substantive stop creates a plum-blossom morning → cherry-blossom afternoon arc, with Bulguksa as the cultural pivot. The 14:45 arrival lands in afternoon-into-golden-hour light on the cherry blossoms reflected in the lake — the most photogenic window of the day.

practicalAccordionItems.title: What's included
practicalAccordionItems.content: Round-trip transport from Busan, bilingual (English / Korean) tour leader, all parking and toll fees, vehicle insurance. All three default attraction stops are free admission: Tongdosa main grounds, Bulguksa Temple, and Bomun Lake. Wondong Plum Village access is also free. Pay-direct: lunch (₩10,000–20,000 per person), optional Tongdosa Seongbo Museum (~₩2,000–3,000), optional Bomun Lake bike or paddle-boat rental (~₩10,000/3hr tandem).

practicalAccordionItems.title: Pickup & drop-off
practicalAccordionItems.content: Three Busan pickup points: Busan Station (KTX) main exit at 08:00, Seomyeon Station Exit 7 at 08:15, Nopo Station Exit 3 at 08:30. Nopo is the nearest Busan subway station to Tongdosa (~25 min drive), which is why it serves as the third pickup on this Yangsan-first day. Choose the station closest to your hotel at booking. Drop-offs in reverse order: Nopo ~17:15, Seomyeon ~17:30, Busan Station ~17:45 — total tour duration ~8.5 hours. Pickup times are not flexible (fixed group shuttle).

practicalAccordionItems.title: Walking & terrain
practicalAccordionItems.content: Moderate. Total walking ~4–6 km across the day. Tongdosa has a 1.2 km riverside paved trail (flat, can go barefoot per VisitKorea) plus temple courtyards across hillside slopes with some stairs. Bulguksa has stone steps between the temple terraces — the lower 33-step bridges are preserved as viewing features and the visitor route uses a sloped path that bypasses them. Bomun Lake is flat 8 km paved loop, stroller- and wheelchair-friendly (the tour samples a 1–2 km segment). Comfortable closed-toe walking shoes are essential.

practicalAccordionItems.title: Vehicle, group size, and accessibility
practicalAccordionItems.content: Mid-size shuttle van or 25-seat coach depending on group size; air-conditioned. Typical group: 8–20 passengers, with a bilingual tour leader narrating between stops. Children 36 months and under ride free (sharing seat with parent). Wheelchair and stroller travelers — please notify at booking. Tongdosa's riverside approach and Bomun Lake are accessible-friendly; Bulguksa's stone steps and Tongdosa's hillside courtyards are partially accessible only.

practicalAccordionItems.title: Spring-only — wider season than a cherry-only tour
practicalAccordionItems.content: Operating dates are approximately Feb 25 – Apr 10 each year. This is a wider span than a cherry-only Gyeongju tour because the Yangsan plum stops (Tongdosa Jajangmae, Wondong Plum Village) add a 3-week earlier-season option. Plum (매화) peak is typically Mar 1–15; cherry (벚꽃) peak is typically Mar 28 – Apr 10; mid-season days (~Mar 15–28) catch both seasons simultaneously. If both plum and cherry are materially delayed or finished and the day cannot deliver meaningful blossoms, the tour is cancelled with at least 3 days' notice and a full refund.

practicalAccordionItems.title: Cancellation
practicalAccordionItems.content: Free cancellation up to 24 hours before pickup. Same-day cancellations and no-shows are non-refundable. If the operator cancels (force majeure, severe weather, both blossom seasons missed), full refund.

practicalAccordionItems.title: What to bring & weather
practicalAccordionItems.content: Late February to early April spans winter→spring transition: 0–18°C with highly variable conditions. Plum blossoms tolerate cold better than cherry; cherry is more rain-sensitive. Both are wind-sensitive — heavy gusts can knock petals off in 24 hours. Bring layers (warm jacket morning, lighter mid-day in late season), a light rain shell (Korea spring rain is common), comfortable walking shoes, a charged camera/phone with portable battery (this is a photography-heavy day), and some cash for lunch (some Wondong greenhouse restaurants are cash-preferred).

staticQuestions.question: What's the difference between this tour and the cherry-only Gyeongju tour?
staticQuestions.answer: This tour has a wider season (Feb 25 – Apr 10 vs Mar 28 – Apr 10 cherry-only), adds Yangsan stops (Tongdosa Temple UNESCO Sansa + Wondong Plum Village), and delivers BOTH plum and cherry blossoms depending on date. The cherry-only tour focuses entirely on Gyeongju and is the better fit if your dates fall squarely in late-March cherry peak. Pick this dual-season tour if you want flexibility, two UNESCO temples, or you're traveling earlier in March when only plum is blooming.

staticQuestions.question: When exactly does each season peak?
staticQuestions.answer: Plum (매화) typically peaks ~Mar 1–15 — Tongdosa Jajangmae and Wondong Village are at full bloom. Cherry (벚꽃) typically peaks ~Mar 28 – Apr 10 — Bulguksa cherry blossom road and Bomun Lake are at full bloom. Mid-season days (~Mar 15–28) often see both seasons together and are the highest-value date range for this tour. Exact dates shift ±7–10 days year to year based on winter temperature; we monitor KMA bloom forecasts and confirm operating dates from mid-February (plum) and mid-March (cherry).

staticQuestions.question: Why is Tongdosa special — and why does it not have a Buddha image?
staticQuestions.answer: Tongdosa is one of Korea's Three Jewel Temples, representing the Buddha himself (the other two are Haeinsa for the Dharma and Songgwangsa for the Sangha). Master Jajang founded it in 646 CE after returning from Tang China bearing genuine relics of the historical Buddha — a robe, a begging bowl, and a bone fragment. Those relics are enshrined in the Diamond Stairway behind Daeungjeon, which is why the main hall's altar faces outward toward the relics rather than holding a Buddha statue. It's also a UNESCO 'Sansa, Buddhist Mountain Monasteries' site since 2018.

staticQuestions.question: What is the Jajangmae plum tree?
staticQuestions.answer: Jajangmae (지장매) is a 350+ year-old red plum tree at Tongdosa Temple, named after the founding master Jajang. In Korean Buddhist tradition it is called the 'first messenger of spring' because it blooms in late February to early March, several weeks before Korea's cherry blossoms. Photographers travel from across Korea to capture the red blossoms against the temple's wooden eaves at dawn. Peak bloom is the centerpiece of the plum-season half of this tour.

staticQuestions.question: How does the Bomun Lake cherry blossom loop work?
staticQuestions.answer: Bomun Lake is encircled by an 8 km flat paved loop trail with ~2,800 cherry trees that form one of Korea's most photographed cherry tunnels during the last week of March and first week of April. The tour samples a 1.5–2 km segment on foot — Bomunjeong Pavilion, the lakeside path, Watermill Square with the 'History of Tourism in Korea Begins Here' plaque, and the artificial waterfall. Optional paddle boat or tandem-bike rentals (~₩10,000/3hr) are available if you'd like water-level photos.

staticQuestions.question: Are admissions included?
staticQuestions.answer: All three default attraction stops are free: Tongdosa main grounds (free), Bulguksa Temple (free since 2023 under the revised Cultural Heritage Protection Act), and Bomun Lake (free outdoor access). Wondong Plum Village access is also free. Optional out-of-pocket items: lunch (₩10,000–20,000 per person), Tongdosa Seongbo Museum (~₩2,000–3,000), Bomun Lake bike or paddle-boat rental (~₩10,000/3hr tandem). Typical pay-direct total ~₩15,000–25,000 per person.

staticQuestions.question: What is Minari Samgyeopsal? What does lunch cost?
staticQuestions.answer: Minari Samgyeopsal is a Yangsan-area seasonal specialty: thick-cut samgyeopsal pork belly grilled tableside and wrapped in fresh raw minari (Korean water-celery / dropwort), available only during plum/minari season at Wondong Village's greenhouse pop-up restaurants. A meal runs ~₩15,000–20,000 per person. During cherry season the lunch shifts to a Gyeongju local restaurant — typically ssambap (rice-and-leaf wraps) at ~₩13,000–18,000. Vegetarian, halal, or gluten-free substitutes (bibimbap or hansik buffet) can be arranged on request — please notify at booking.

staticQuestions.question: How accessible is Tongdosa for older travelers, wheelchairs, or strollers?
staticQuestions.answer: The 1.2 km riverside paved trail to the temple is flat and accessible — VisitKorea notes that visitors can even go barefoot. The temple grounds spread across hillside slopes with some stairs, so the central courtyards are partially accessible only. Bomun Lake is fully stroller- and wheelchair-friendly. Bulguksa has more stone steps; the lower 33-step bridges are preserved as viewing features and the visitor path uses a sloped route that bypasses them. Children 36 months and under ride free.

staticQuestions.question: What if it rains?
staticQuestions.answer: Light spring rain: tour operates as planned (cherry blossoms in light mist actually photograph beautifully). Heavy rain: Tongdosa's hillside courtyards and Bulguksa's stone become slippery; the guide may shorten outdoor time and extend covered space. Heavy gusts can knock blossom petals off in 24 hours, so wind matters as much as rain. Severe weather warnings: the operator will offer rebooking or a full refund. If both blossom seasons miss with at least 3 days' notice, full refund.

staticQuestions.question: Is this a good choice for first-time visitors who want spring blossoms in Korea?
staticQuestions.answer: Yes. It pairs Korea's two most iconic spring blooms (plum and cherry) with two UNESCO Buddhist temples in a single day from Busan, with no double-backing on the route. First-time visitors who want both flowers and heritage content from a Busan base are the primary audience for this product.

staticQuestions.question: How much walking is there?
staticQuestions.answer: ~4–6 km total. Tongdosa has the longest single walk (1.2 km flat riverside trail in + temple courtyards). Bulguksa is moderate — stone steps and slopes between terraces. Bomun Lake is flat and easy (the tour samples 1–2 km of the 8 km loop). Comfortable closed-toe walking shoes are essential, especially because Korean spring rain can make stone surfaces slippery.

staticQuestions.question: Is this suitable for families with children?
staticQuestions.answer: Yes for school-age children (~8+) who can handle a full-day rhythm. The plum and cherry blossom photography, the Tongdosa pine-forest approach, and the Bomun Lake paddle boats are all kid-friendly. Younger children may find the temple sites quiet; the bilingual tour leader can simplify the Buddhist history content for them.

staticQuestions.question: Can older adults join comfortably?
staticQuestions.answer: Recommended for active seniors comfortable with 4–6 km of walking. The Tongdosa riverside trail is flat and barefoot-friendly per VisitKorea. Bomun Lake is wheelchair- and stroller-friendly. Bulguksa has stone steps but the visitor path bypasses the steepest sections. Travelers using a cane manage the route; wheelchair users should consider a private tour for full route adjustments.

staticQuestions.question: What's the recommended minimum age?
staticQuestions.answer: Best fit is around age 8 and up. Children 36 months and under ride free (sharing seat with parent). Younger children can join but should be comfortable with a full 8.5-hour day and plenty of walking outdoors.
